speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been very much interested in what has been said by some hon. members who have spoken on this motion. I appreciate the fact that I shall have another opportunity to meet with my colleagues to discuss the affairs of the Canadian National Railways. I was sorry that I was attending the meeting of a committee when the minister made his cheerful statement concerning the past and the coming year in relation to the operations of the Canadian National Railways.
The committee we are now asked to set up is a very useful one. It is only fair that members of parliament who vote moneys by way of subsidies for the support of the Canadian National Railways should be entitled to some information concerning the expenditures of that organization. At times there are some complications. We are told that the company should follow the usual rule in business, that of rendering an account to members of parliament.
Committee on Railways and Shipping
The case of the railways is a peculiar one. In the first place I wish to tell the genial Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) that, as always, he can rely upon my support. But it would be well for the officials of the railways to realize that members of parliament are in duty bound to exercise certain controls in respect of the way the railways are administered. That is only fair. We are asked questions by our constituents, and when we are not in a position to answer they are stunned; they cannot understand it. Therefore I hope the officials of the railways will realize that instead of having any bad feeling toward them, each time members of parliament attend sittings of the committee on railways and shipping and ask questions it is for the purpose of helping those officials in the administration of the railways. We do not ask those questions to cause trouble. Some officials seem to be under the false impression that when members of parliament ask questions they are opposing the railways. This is not so; we are trying to help them, and it is unfortunate that sometimes the officials do not seem to understand this.
Sometimes decisions made should be more carefully considered beforehand-and I am thinking of the closing of some shops. The railways should consider the effect of this action on the communities concerned. As the Canadian National Railways are supported by the people of Canada, the officials of that system must give consideration to our people in all their dealings. I am not going to insist upon this at great length, because I am sure the Minister of Transport does not miss any opportunities to remind the railway officials of their duty. And so much the better for them. The officials may not like it, as sometimes they do not seem to like the questions asked in committee by members of parliament, but some good comes from that questioning. Fortunately members of parliament realize that decisions have been taken at times too quickly, and that something must be done by way of compensation. This is particularly true of my own county, and I am thanking the government for what was done.
The Canadian National Railways has a long history. At first it was a government railway. The Intercolonial was operated under the direction of the minister of railways; and older employees and members of their families are still under the impression that the government is in control. That is not the case, but it is in their minds.
I know the purpose of the minister is to leave the railway board free to administer the railways to the best of their ability. This
3122	HOUSE OF
Committee on Railways and Shipping has been government policy for a long time. On the other hand members of parliament are responsible for what is done by the Canadian National Railways, and because of that we are entitled to make observations for their benefit. I am not going to complain about what has been done in the past; I am concerned with the present and the future of the railways and their employees.
Very often we see officers of the railways, now grown in importance, who asked us when they were in smaller jobs for our support to gain promotions. But as soon as they get their promotions they say, "No politics with the railways; we are above politicians; we do not want politicians to interfere". To get. their promotions they held us by the sleeve. That is the story of human nature. They were not independent when they wanted something. They got it, under false pretences; and now they seem to be very independent and give us the cold shoulder. They will not listen to what we say, not on their behalf but on behalf of the railways.
Human nature is weak. Some errors may be committed by humble employees of the railway as well as by those in high office.
I am not going to insist upon this point, but I am sure all hon. members know what I mean. Why be so hard on a man with a family who may have made a mistake but who, in doing so, caused no damage to the railways, and who would like to be reinstated? Those questions should be reconsidered, because the ones who have suffered an injustice have the sympathy of the community.
With reference to the pension paid to old employees of the Intercolonial, it will be recalled that some time ago engineers, conductors, brakemen and firemen were paid only $1.25. They were paid a very small salary. The pensions of some of the employees of the Canadian National Railways are based on that salary. The government has contributed an amount to the provident fund of the railway and I hope it will be increased as a matter of justice to help those employees who were good servants of the railway at a time when the railway was administered by the minister of railways and canals. It is with the best disposition and the friendliest spirit that I am conveying these remarks through you, sir, to the Minister of Transport.
If the officials of the railways read Hansard, they will realize that all that has been said here has been said for their own good and that of the railways.

speechtext:
I do not propose to speak at any length on this occasion, but I wanted to say, as others before me have said, how much interested those of us are who are members of this particular committee. We do gain from that experience a great deal of useful information by firsthand reports from the gentlemen who are the heads respectively of the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian National Steamships and Trans-Canada Air Lines. I recall that from the work of the committee last year and the year before I myself gained quite a bit of important information from hearing these firsthand reports.
There is no doubt that western Canada has as great an interest in railway problems as has any part of this country, and more than most parts because we are so dependent upon the railway. We have not the shipping facilities that are enjoyed by the east and the west coasts and by central Canada with its great lakes system. To us then in western Canada the railway system ranks as the most important link for us with the rest of the world. The importance of the railway system in western Canada is easily observed from a map showing the extent of the railway system stretching for so many hundreds of miles and criss-crossing the great western prairie country where such abundant crops are grown. Now we find the development of the railway system stretching farther and farther northward, notably recently into the northern parts of the province of Manitoba in connection with the mineral developments at Lynn Lake. Therefore, so far as western Canada is concerned, the problem of the railways ranks of the highest importance. And throughout the years people from western Canada have very naturally taken an interest in the railways and their problems.
We are very much concerned with the question of freight rates and watch that problem with a great deal of interest. We naturally hope that when the C.N.R. makes its annual report it will indicate a profit and not a loss, because if a series of losses occur annually then the freight rate question comes to the fore, and in the last few years we have seen the circumstances surrounding that problem and the great increase in freight rates since the war, imposing an additional burden on the producers in western Canada and the consumers in that area.
From our point of view since we grow huge crops of wheat and other grains which must be disposed of in large part on the world markets, freight rates rank as a matter

of major importance. Those of us who come from western Canada view with a measure of alarm, certainly with regret, the fact that the issue of the Crowsnest pass rates on grain is raised from time to time and not discussed in its fullest implications. The impression is erroneously conveyed to the public that that rate that was set a great many years ago is not now applicable under modern conditions. The erroneous aspect of the argument is that attention is not paid to the enormous increase in volume of traffic to which those Crowsnest pass rates apply, and the railways are benefiting from the development of the west and of the crop areas and from the tremendous development in the volume of grain shipped over our railways. Consequently, those of us from western Canada have to keep a wary eye on all matters in connection with freight rates.
We shall be interested in hearing the report of the president of the Canadian National Railways with regard to the effect of the changes in freight rates on the business of the railways, the effect in so far as the subsidy is concerned that was provided last year for the so-called bridge between the east and the west north of the great lakes. These and other problems will likely be brought to the attention of the president of the Canadian National Railways, and I hope we will get complete answers, as we have in other years got complete answers, on virtually all the problems raised.
I am sure there will be an interesting discussion with regard to the passenger traffic on the railway and its comparison in the subsequent report that we shall receive from the Trans-Canada Air Lines with the increase in passenger traffic of the air lines. I think I recall last year the prediction on the part of the air lines that the great majority of passenger traffic would soon be via air, and its effect therefore on the railways is a matter of considerable importance.
We got from the T.C.A. an equally able report on the development of that method of transportation, and that adds to the interest of the committee. 1 have just one final word to say. I note that the minister himself is not on the committee this year.
I was wondering whether he was going to come on. Last year he was not placed on the committee at first, but later he was put on. It is of interest to me because of the fact that in the house, when questions are asked concerning these institutions, we are referred to the Canadian National Railways itself and to the Trans-Canada Air Lines. It is not easy to see the division of responsibility as far as the government is concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief, because judging from the contributions in the debate thus far it would appear to me that the affairs of the Canadian National Railways are in good hands and are operated satisfactorily, since on the whole there has been little or no criticism in the course of the discussion this afternoon. There are a number of things which have been brought to the attention of the government during the course of this debate, but it is not possible for me to deal with them all. However, I feel I must at least give some attention to one or two of the matters that have come under discussion. It is impossible, of course, to deal with all the suggestions or points made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), but there are one or two matters with which he dealt which I would like to take a few moments to discuss.
One had to do with freight rates and that was also discussed by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) who has just resumed his seat. The position with reference to freight rates as regards western Canada and even the country as a whole is far better now than it has been for some time. I do not mean, of course, with reference to the general impact upon the cost of transportation, but with regard to the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation.
The recommendations of the royal commission on transportation have been implemented almost in their entirety, save for one or two exceptions. Dealing generally with freight rates, following the recommendations of the commission parliament enacted changes and introduced amendments to the Railway Act. One of them was to ask the board of transport commissioners to make an investigation with reference to the equalization of rates. That has been done in part, and a recent order has been issued by the board of transport commissioners equalizing the rates whereby the amount of differential was reduced or made to disappear making freight rates in the whole of
3124	HOUSE OF
Committee on Railways and Shipping western Canada from the Pacific coast to the Ontario boundary almost equal. Class rates in the east and west were brought closer together by an earlier order of the board which had the effect of reducing them in western Canada by 5 per cent, and increasing them in eastern Canada by about 10 per cent.
The bridge subsidy brought in two years ago, following the recommendations of the royal commission, covered a subsidy of $7 million concerning the bridge from Capreol through Sudbury, and on through to the head of the lakes to the west. The effect of that subsidy of $7 million, payable to the railways for the maintenance of their trackage, has been to reduce east-west rates by about 8 per cent.
Then the one and one-third rule was brought into effect by virtue of an amendment to the Railway Act which had an effect on all the western provinces, particularly Saskatchewan, Alberta, and a large part of British Columbia, and they received the benefit of the transcontinental rate plus one-third. Most of the recommendations of the royal commission in that respect have been implemented.
The other two matters to which I wish to direct my attention are the conditions of employment on the Canadian National Railways, and the question of pensions. Unemployment on the Canadian National Railways and the so-called lay-offs have not been nearly as serious as the house was perhaps led to believe during the earlier part of the session. I would like to place on record some of the figures which are pertinent to this issue. For example, in 1939 the average number of employees in the Canadian National Railways was 78,129. In 1951 that had climbed to 121,191, and in 1952, the last year for which figures are available, the total was 127,930.
The total payroll for 1939 was $122 million. For 1951 it was $381,654,000 and in 1952 it was $405,541,000. The average earnings per employee in 1939 was $1,500, roughly speaking. In 1951 that had almost doubled to $3,149, and in 1952 the average earnings per employee in the Canadian National Railways was $3,170.
With reference to lay-offs I have figures covering the period up to January 31, 1954. The total of 1,492 covers the reduction in the mechanical department staff at the main shops throughout Canada. The breakdown is as follows: In the Montreal shops 427; in the Atlantic region 248; in the central region 268; and in the western region 549. The reason why the western region total is larger than


the others is because it concerns four provinces, and has to do with the shops at Trans-cona, Fort Rouge, Calder and Port Mann. Therefore, the total lay-off in the mechanical staff department was 1,492.
Generally speaking the total lay-offs in the Canadian National Railways in all spheres of activity amounted to 6,400 employees. These can be broken down into 2,200 maintenance of way men, 2,300 mechanical staff, and 1,900 others. While I include maintenance of way men who had been laid off at the end of January 1954, I should add that I know that since then many of them have been taken on again because these men are laid off and taken on dependent on the work that is being contemplated, so that whether we include the total number, or whether we only give the number in the mechanical shops, it is a very small proportion of the employment figure for 1952 which I gave a moment ago, namely 127,930 employees. What were the reasons for this? I would just like to take a few moments to give some of the reasons, and some of the hopes for the future.
The railway business is dependent upon the general activity in transportation services in the country as a whole. I said on an earlier occasion and I repeat now that the operations of the Canadian National Railways compare favourably with those of any other on the North American continent, and with those of the sister railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway. The decline in traffic is because of a drop in international traffic, that is traffic which is connected with Canadian National Railways at the boundary line, and also in the United States branch of the Canadian National Railways operated south of the border.
There has also been a reduction in the level of activity because of the extended use of diesel locomotives. These locomotives have been put into operation substantially in western Canada. Steam locomotives are being supplanted by oil burning equipment. The position in the maritimes I know is a serious one and causes much concern to all hon. members from that part of the country. However, due to certain conditions, which the president of the Canadian National Railways mentioned during the sittings of the committee last year, the program in that part of the country is on a longer term basis than that in western Canada.
Those features, namely the current level of traffic, particularly in the last four or five months, from September last year to the end of December of this year, are fully responsible for these lay-offs or reductions

in employment. However, I am happy to say that for the present year, namely the early months of 1954, the figures indicate a slight improvement in the activities of the Canadian National Railways. I am informed that it is anticipated the physical volume of business in 1954 will not be too far removed from what it was in 1953. In fact, I do not think it will be much more than 1 per cent less than it was last year. That would indicate the soundness of the economy of the country as well as the stability of the operations of the Canadian National Railways.
I turn to this much discussed question of pensions. I would not want the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to think that he is alone in the advocacy of increased pensions for retired employees or present employees of the Canadian National Railways. If I have ever given the impression in this house that such was the case, I want to correct it immediately because there are coming into my office letters from members of parliament from all sides of the house, and more particularly from this side of it, making themselves advocates of the pensioners, retired or otherwise, of the Canadian National Railways. However, I think that the house is not fully conversant with this position. Perhaps the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) is the one who, in his discussion of it, put his finger on the circumstances as I understand them.
In order fully to understand the pension position of the employees of the Canadian National Railways, I think it is important that we go back somewhat to ascertain and to see what happened in past years. In order fully to appreciate the implications of the railway's basic pension plan of $25 per month, it is essential to go back to before 1935. Prior to that time, that is January 1, 1935, the Canadian National pension plan was based upon the former Grand Trunk Railway pension plan which provided generally a pension to employees on the attainment of age 65, equivalent to one per cent of the employee's highest ten-year average salary, multiplied by the number of years of service. A careful study born of the depression in the years immediately preceding 1935 demonstrated to management that the Canadian National system should no longer sustain the financial burden of this "free" pension plan.
However, since employees then on the Canadian National payroll were considered to have some moral right to protection against a revision in the plan under which they had previously been working, the 1935 amendments undertook, among other things, to provide a service pension calculated on the basis of 83276-198
Committee on Railways and Shipping the former Grand Trunk plan up to January 1, 1935, with a guaranteed contractual basic pension of $25 per month in any event. Thus the 1935 rules, as regards service prior to that date, preserved the former scale of free pension benefits to all employees and, through the medium of the guaranteed minimum, improved the position of many.
The next point I wish to make is that subsequent to 1935 those who were willing to pay approximately one-half of the cost of pensions arising from service after that date were afforded an opportunity to increase their pension benefits. Thus, an employee is permitted under the 1935 rules to supplement his free pension by contributions up to 10 per cent of his compensation, such contribution, with interest, being matched by the company to a maximum of 5 per cent of that compensation, with the company further guaranteeing that if the employee makes a 5 per cent contribution his pension will not be less than that payable to him under the former rules.
As regards employees who joined the service subsequent to January 1, 1935, the company provided a free pension of $25 a month which the employee was privileged to improve by contributions as aforesaid. The revised 1935 plan thus consisted of a small free pension plus a supplemental annuity on a money purchase basis within the aforesaid limits. It is therefore apparent that the Canadian National employee had only to contribute his share to the fund to obtain a pension considerably higher than $25 per month. It should be remembered also that he would have made no contribution in respect of the $25, and that the company would make a substantial contribution to the supplemental annuity if he took advantage of that offer.
Despite the provisions made for increased pension benefits, based on voluntary contributions, many employees obviously preferred the non-contributory guaranteed basic pension only. I am informed by the Canadian National management that in spite of periodic campaigns by management and labour representatives who supported the revised provisions the number of actual contributors has been disappointing. Out of 114,028 Canadian employees eligible to contribute only 41,828 had elected to do so as of December 31, 1953.
At January 1, 1952, some 3,200 retired Canadian National Railways employees, as has been said here, were receiving the basic pension of $25 per month. At July 1, 1952, there were, over and above that number, 190 former Canadian government railway employees, retired under the provident fund act, who were receiving the minimum pension of $30 a month. CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS Office of the Chairman and President
Effective 1 Jan. 1952
Montreal, March 7, 1952
To all Officers and Employees:
The employees will have seen from my "23" message, dated March 5th, and references in the press, that the directors have made some revisions to the existing Canadian National Railways pension plan. As advance information for the employees there is given below a short description of the plan as revised. The detailed rules and regulations will be completed in due course, printed in booklet form, and a copy furnished to every employee.
The description given below will give the employees a fairly good idea regarding the provisions of the revised plan but employees approaching retirement age, particularly if they are contributing to the pension fund, are advised to communicate with the superintendent of pensions who will furnish to them such additional information they may need to exercise the options which are available to them. It will be appreciated that it is not possible in such a brief description to set out every detail of so comprehensive a pension plan, and it must be understood that the actual rules will be the governing factor in determining eligibility for and the amount of pensions.
D. Gordon
Chairman and President.
Short description of a revised pension plan for Canadian National Railways
The revised plan is in two parts.
Part 1 is the existing plan with some amendments designed to make better provision for present and future employees who become disabled, and also for early retirement. It provides a basic pension of $25 per month at the expense of the company, and also for a supplemental pension at the joint expense of the company and the employee. It is optional with the employee whether he contributes or not. He may contribute an even percentage of his compensation from 1 per cent to 10 per cent and the company will match his contributions after 10 years service but not in excess of 5 per cent. The amount of the supplemental pension is that which the joint contributions with compound interest will buy. The plan makes provision for benefits for service prior to 1935 when the present contributory plan was established.
The employee may select the type of pension he wishes, that is to say he may elect to take it in the form of an annuity payable during his life time, or payable during his life time but guaranteed in any event for either 5, 10, or 15 years, or in the form of a joint life and last survivor annuity. The amount of a guaranteed or survivor type annuity is of course less than the single life annuity but is the actuarial equivalent of the single life annuity.
As amended the plan provides pensions for disabled employees provided they have attained age 50 with not less than 20 years service. If the portion of the pension payable at the expense of the company is less than $40 per month (on a single life basis) the company will grant a special disability allowance so as to increase its portion of the pension to $40 until the employee reaches age 65. If an employee with these age and service requirements should die in service the pension board may grant a survivor benefit equal to one half the amount of such employee's pension, on a single life basis, but excluding the allowance referred to. Such benefit

will be payable during the life time of a surviving spouse, or for 10 years from the date of the employee's retirement, whichever period is longer.
Normal retirement is at age 65 with 20 years service, but provision is made for early retirement with reduced pensions. For each year below age 65, one additional year's service will be required, so that an employee may retire at age 64 with 21 years service or age 55 with 30 years service, or anywhere in between where the age and years of service add to 85.
The optional and flexible provisions of part 1 are considered by many employees to be preferable to a more rigid compulsory contributory plan. It allows employees considerable freedom to shape their railway pension to their needs as they see them.
Part 2 is designed to meet the requirements of those who wish to obtain larger pensions and who are willing to join a plan under which contributions are compulsory. Employees will be covered by part 1 unless they elect to transfer to part 2, which election will be irrevocable. They will be given ample time to make their election.
Under this part the employee must contribute 5 per cent of his compensation and the company will pay the balance of the cost. The pension will be a percentage, based on length of allowable service, of the employee's average compensation during the last 5 or 10 years of service whichever is more favorable to the employee. The percentage will be 1 per cent for each year of service up to 20 years, li per cent for each year during the next 10 years, and \\ per cent for each year over 30 years service. Fractions of a year will be computed proportionately. This pension will be payable during the life time of the employee. On the decease of the employee one half the pension will be payable during the life time of a surviving spouse, or for 10 years from the date of the employee's retirement, whichever period is the longer.
A provision is also made for pensions to disabled employees. These benefits are available to employees who have attained age 50, who have at least 20 years allowable service, and who are certified by the company's chief medical offcer to be unfitted for further service by reason of permanent physical or mental disability. If an employee with these age and service requirements should die in service the pension board may grant a survivor benefit similar in terms to the one referred to in the preceding paragraph.
The normal retirement date is age 65 but a provision is made for early retirement with reduced pensions, the age and service requirements being similar to those referred to under part 1.
The pension benefits are conditional on the employee having paid 5 per cent of his compensation throughout the period of his service from January 1st, 1935 or from the date he last entered the service if entry was later than January 1st, 1935, until the date of his retirement. An employee whose total contributions prior to date of transfer are less than the required amount will be permitted to make good the arrears during his remaining service by additional contributions, or lump sum payments, but if arrears are not made good the pension will be reduced proportionately.
An employee who transfers from part 1 to part 2 and who had contributed under the existing plan in excess of 5 per cent of his compensation, will receive repayment for the amount of the excess.
That position was recognized by the general chairman of the association of the men when he wrote to Mr. Cooper, the chairman of the pension fund of the Canadian National Railways, thanking him for the benefit of the assistance that was given by the officers of 83276-198i
Committee on Railways and Shipping the Canadian National Railways in connection with this plan. I should like to put that on Hansard but I do not have the time. I refer to it and it can be found at page 112 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the sessional committee on railways and shipping of Tuesday, April 29, 1952. But I commend that letter to the consideration of the house. It indicates surely that the railways have given this matter careful consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. In tonight's press I see a report by the Canadian Press to the effect that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) had stated that I wished Canada unilaterally to raise the price of gold in Canada. This so shocked me, as it is the very antithesis of everything I have said on the subject for many years, that I ask the right for complete and absolute denial at the earliest possible occasion-which is now.
What I advocate now, as in the past, is not that Canada set a price for gold, but that she, as the world's third trading nation, establish a free market for gold in Canada, so that an acceptable price may be arrived at, based on the open market decision within a country not employing exchange or currency control. This is the whole basis of my argument about gold as a monetary unit, and as an agent of convertibility. I introduced a bill this session on this very point.
I regret I had to be out of the house in the dying minutes of the debate on gold, and I regret that my point was not understood about the free market. I hope the minister will understand this-and I see he is in the house. I know he did not misstate the point deliberately, but I wish to correct it now. What I said in the debate on the bill was that Canada should take the lead and establish a free market for gold, so that a price could be arrived at within a free economy- not that we could artificially peg the price at $50, or any other amount, which would be quite impossible.
I agree with the minister in what he said. I wish merely to correct any misunderstanding, because his suggestion is the very antithesis of everything I have said in the house for years.
[Mr. Knowles.)

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not quite concluded my remarks yesterday afternoon at the dinner adjournment. It is always a temptation, when one's remarks in any debate are divided into two instalments, to repeat on the second occasion much of what was said on the first. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I intend as best I can to resist that temptation.
However, there is one observation I must make in regard to one point I was seeking to emphasize yesterday. I referred to a form of export control which the government had made use of when, on December 14, 1953, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) announced that the Canadian government had undertaken to limit the shipment of Canadian oats to the United States to 23 million bushels during the period from midnight December 10, 1953, to midnight September 30, 1954.
I said that that action was taken by the Canadian government in view of an imminent breach by the United States congress of the principles of GATT. I see that in the Canadian Press despatch reporting my remarks yesterday the comment follows that I did not say what that breach would be. Let me take that up and make quite clear what that breach of the principles of GATT on the part of the United States congress would be.
The explanation is to be found at page 861 of Hansard in the statement made to the house on December 14 last by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. His statement proceeds:
We have now been advised that the tariff commission-
That is, the tariff commission of the United States.
-has made its report to the President and that this report recommends restrictions on imports of oats into the United States. It was. of course, hoped that the President would not find it necessary to act

upon this report. It can he taKen for granted that both governments wish, if possible, to avoid getting into restrictions and counter-restrictions.
The imminent breach of the principles of GATT to which I referred was the threat that the United States congress would act at that moment to impose restrictions upon the importation of Canadian oats into the United States. Canada has supplied practically all the oats imported into the United States market. This is a matter of high importance to the Canadian producers of oats. What I complained of then, and most emphatically complain of today, is that the Canadian government should apply restrictions upon the export of Canadian oats to the United States with a view to forfending, apparently, the imposition of restrictions by the United States congress on the importation of Canadian oats into that country.
If the United States congress is determined again to commit a breach of the spirit and letter of the general agreement on tariffs and trade then the responsibility for that breach should be left precisely where it belongs-on the shoulders of the United States congress. And it is highly improper for the Canadian government, in the exercise of the power it possesses under the Export and Import Permits Act, or any other statute, to come to the rescue of the United States congress in that situation and impose export restrictions upon Canadian producers of oats.
We were not told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he made this statement in the house on December 14, what was the statutory authority under which the government was proceeding. One can only infer that it must have been the Export and Import Permits Act, which is being replaced by the measure now under debate. But whatever the authority was, I say that it was an improper exercise of that authority on the part of the Canadian government.
I had also dealt yesterday with a question which is coming to the fore in the capitals of not a few countries in the west, that of trade with Russia-trade, not simply in strategic materials, but the whole question of trading relationships with Russia. I reviewed what had been said in the United Kingdom recently in that regard. May I refer to a dispatch emanating from one other European capital on the same subject. It is a dispatch from Brussels under date of January 31, and contains this announcement:
Belgium and Russia today signed a new trade agreement worth 5,000,000,000 Belgian francs ($100,000,000) in trade to each country.
Russia will export to Belgium and Luxembourg cereals, small cars, celluloses, manganese, chromium, coal, tar, asbestos, cast iron, furs, tobacco, canned goods and other products.
Export and Import Permits Act
Belgium will supply Russia with textiles, fish, vegetable oils, hides and skins, lead and chemicals as well as other products. In addition Belgium is to construct 10 cargo vessels, 10 cold storage ships, floating cranes and other marine equipment to be delivered to Russia over the coming three years.
The volume of trade under the new agreement is double that of last year.
In view of what is being said from London and from Moscow these days on this subject, and in view also of reports such as the one I have just read, I ask again in this house: what is the position of the Canadian government with reference to this subject of trade with Russia? It is one thing to restrict export of strategic materials, anything that by any stretch of the imagination could be of assistance to a nation that may be bent on aggression. There is no one in this house who would give anything to any aggressor nation that would be of the slightest assistance in furthering the aggressive intent of any such nation. But I think we should know what is the policy of the Canadian government on the subject of trade with Russia.
Now, sir, I wish to speak on another aspect of trade in relation to a bill that deals with attempts to control the export of what are called strategic materials. This is a rather different subject because, although it relates principally to any nation behind the iron curtain, it is a nation, in view of the United Nations' action, which is in a different category. I refer to China.
Trade with China is restricted, as the house will recall, under a resolution passed by the security council of the United Nations back in June, 1950, immediately following the violation of the border of South Korea when the communist aggressors burst over it and sought to overrun the southern part of the peninsula. That resolution of the United Nations has been binding upon Canada as a loyal member of the United Nations. Under that resolution Canada as a member is bound to prevent shipments of munitions and arms to China or to any intermediate country through which such shipments might eventually reach China.
As long as our relations with the United Nations are such as they are, and as long as relations of the United Nations are such as they are with Red China, I urge, Mr. Speaker, that it should be made quite clear that Canada will stand firmly behind her obligations as a member of the United Nations and behind that resolution. We do not wish to contemplate that the present situation may last forever. It is only a cease-fire that exists in Korea today. No one who hopes seriously for better days can contemplate that this situation can continue indefinitely in Korea. But, Mr. Speaker, as long as Red China stands in the category of an aggressor,

Export and Import Permits Act branded as such by a finding of the United Nations, then I submit that it is the duty of Canada as a loyal member of the United Nations to stand firmly behind the present resolution which prohibits the sending of arms, munitions and implements of war either to Red China or to any nation through which such material may reach Red China. And similarly, I think that through the United Nations Canada must keep a very close examination upon trade that other nations are carrying on or proposing to carry on with Red China.
I have before me a dispatch coming from the United Nations, New York, dated February 7. It is a little lengthy, Mr. Speaker, but I think that every bit of it is of striking interest in relation to this subject. It reads:
Red China's trade with the non-communist world rose sharply during the first half of 1953, a United Nations survey showed Saturday.
The U.N. figures, published in the monthly bulletin of statistics, showed:
1.	Communist China's exports to the free world increased from $151,100,000 in the first six months of 1952 to $205,100,000 for the corresponding period last year.
2.	Her imports from non-communist countries rose from $112,200,000 in the first half of 1952 to $163,300,000 for the first half of 1953.
3.	Countries increasing their trade with red China included Britain, France, Belgium, West Germany. The Netherlands, the Scandinavian countries, Italy, Austria and Japan.
4.	While communist China's trade with the free world was increasing, the trend of Russia's trade and that of her eastern European satellites was just the opposite. There was a drop in the total trade between communist and non-communist countries of Europe.
Although the total dollar increase in red China's trade with the free world was not substantial when compared with the total volume of world trade, there was a percentage increase of approximately a third in both imports and exports.
The United States and India were the only major countries to have reduced their trade with the Chinese communists.
The table listed red China's exports to the United States for the first half of 1952 at $22,500,000 and those for the first half of 1953 at $4 million. Exports from the United States to communist China were listed at zero for both periods.
Britain's imports from red China rose from $4,500,000 to $10,900,000 and those of British overseas territories increased from $89,700,000 to $120,300,000. Western Europe's total imports from communist China increased from $26,400,000 to $55,400,000.
Britain's exports to red China increased from $1,800,000 to $8,700,000.
May I just observe before leaving that subject, Mr. Speaker, that it is clear that a large number of countries of free western Europe have been increasing their trade with Red China. These are countries that are members of the United Nations. It is quite clear that this trade therefore is not in so-called strategic materials. Nevertheless, I do submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a matter that must have close attention on the part

of the Canadian government. There have been suggestions emanating from Europe that there should be a re-examination of the category of strategic materials with a view to narrowing the list of goods whose export to countries behind the iron curtain is prohibited. This is a matter that should be engaging close attention on the part of a government like our own which has a considerable interest in external trade. Even though we are doing no trade with China ourselves now, Mr. Speaker, we still have the liveliest interest in the matter of the trade of other free nations with China.
It will I am sure be the unanimous view of this house that it is imperative that every reasonable step be taken to prevent strategic materials that could be of any use in the aggressive plans of any nation behind the iron curtain falling into the hands of such a country. But we must have a statement of policy on the part of this government. When this house is asked to vest in the Canadian government very wide powers with reference to the export of Canadian goods as well as to the import of foreign goods into this country, it is imperative that there be a statement from the government and from the minister as to the policy of the government.
I asked, as I mentioned yesterday, on a previous occasion, now six weeks ago, for a statement on the part of the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to the position of the government with reference to trade with Russia. The minister's answers were evasions; but the time for evasion has passed, the time for a statement of policy from the government has come, and this bill should not be allowed to pass through until there has been an adequate and comprehensive statement by this government on its policy with respect to trade with these countries.
It will be recognized, of course, Mr. Speaker, that trade has an important part to play in improving relations between the countries of the world, not only between the western nations but between countries that have been behind the iron curtain and the west. That is the view that is coming to the fore, and more prominently in Europe today. It is most opportune that the Minister of Trade and Commerce returned last night from two days spent in Washington as a member of the Canadian delegation which went there for the purpose of discussing mutual questions in relation to trade. It is therefore appropriate that the house should hear tonight from the Minister of Trade and Commerce in relation to the subject of trade between Canada and the United States, in relation to these questions which are under discussion between the free countries as to

their plans in regard to trade with nations behind the iron curtain, and with respect also to the matter of strategic materials.
Let the house realize that this bill purports to confer very wide powers upon the government. It is an enabling bill. It is a bill which vests very sweeping powers in this government. Many of its provisions are of the kind with which many of us in this house do not agree. They give such wide powers to the government that it would allow this government, if it chose, to use these powers so as to create discrimination between Canadian importers, and also discrimination as between exporters. It puts power into the hands of the Canadian government over wide sections of the whole Canadian economy. Powers of this kind should not be vested in government except under the compulsion of strictly emergent conditions.
That brings me, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, to the matter I raised yesterday. I urged upon the government a course which I believe is highly necessary and opportune. I recalled that when this measure came before the house in 1947, on the suggestion of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell) it was referred to the banking and commerce committee. This subject of export and import control has not been before any parliamentary committee since 1947, seven years ago. There has been no detailed review of the operation of export and import controls by a parliamentary committee in seven years. It is a matter of high importance. The whole structure of our controls is before us again in this bill by which the government seeks not only an extension of those powers in point of time, but an extension of those powers in terms of their nature. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary at this time that the whole structure of the operation of our export and import controls should be submitted to careful study by the banking and commerce committee.
I am well aware as a member of that committee, Mr. Speaker, that the committee has a substantial volume of work before it during this session. It is studying, under reference from this house, amendments to the Bank Act and the Bank of Canada Act, but the indications are that the time these two measures will absorb this year in the committee is not at all comparable with the time that the study of two similar measures occupied in the banking and commerce committee ten years ago, at the time of the last decennial revision of the Bank Act. Therefore, I believe it is quite clear that the banking and commerce committee has time to give this measure, covering the whole of

Export and Import Permits Act our export and import controls structure, the kind of careful review and study it ought to have now.
Let the house remember that there is a provision in this bill which contemplates that the control powers shall be in effect for three years until July 31, 1957. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the house ought not to part with wide powers such as this, to vest special powers of this kind in the executive branch of government for a period of three years, powers which can only be justified on the basis of an existing and present emergency necessitating the taking of energetic measures with respect to what we call strategic materials, without very careful scrutiny. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge that this measure should be sent to that committee for adequate study and for limitation of the period during which this measure is to have effect without further extension.
This is the kind of emergency legislation, and the powers it confers on the government are of a kind, which the house should not confer in any event for more than a year at a time, so that it retains control itself over the executive branch of government and guarantees in that way that it will have returned to it each session for review the measure itself and the actions of the government in pursuance thereof.
There are continuing dangers in a measure of this kind. Let us, in recognizing the fact that great dangers exist, realize that there is a need for effective control over strategic materials, and let us see to it that parliament retains a close check-rein before parting with powers as broad as these.

Mr. Speaker, I thought the hon. member was going to argue with the statement I made that he failed to enunciate the policy of the Conservative party with regard to trade with Russia. Instead, he rises to quarrel as to whether he spoke for an hour and a quarter, an hour and ten minutes or an hour and twelve and a half minutes. Perhaps the speech was made too near their recent convention for the Conservative party to have a policy on trade with Russia. Of course, I think the Liberal party is in the same position when it comes to trade with Russia. When you ask them what their policy is, the Minister of Trade and Commerce who ordinarily does not do much skating, skates around the question and from his reply we really do not know what the government's policy is with regard to trade with Russia.
I should like to see all possible steps taken by the Canadian government to promote an increase in trade in ordinary peacetime goods and goods that have no strategic value. I think that the more trade nations in the west have with nations behind the iron curtain, the less danger there is of a global war. Any action with regard to trade that will raise the living standards of the people in western nations and that would, of course, help to raise the living standards of people in the iron curtain countries is something that I believe is in the interests of all the people of the world and of peace.
I therefore say that the C.C.F. believe that our government should take all possible steps to promote ordinary peacetime trade with the Soviet union. In that respect I might say that we are travelling in very good company. The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, Right Hon. Winston Churchill, in a speech delivered on February 25, emphasized the

importance of increasing trade with Russia as a means, not only of raising the living standards of the people in the nations involved but also as a means of reducing international tension and of promoting peace in the world.
When the hon. member for Eglinton came to discuss trade with China he did not take a neutral, non-committal position as he did in discussing trade with Russia. Instead, he said that a resolution had been passed by the United Nations banning trade with Red China and that he felt that no such trade should be undertaken. I can agree with that statement as far as it goes. But I believe the time is coming when steps must be taken to open peacetime trade with China.
The Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) has returned from a tour around the world. I am sure that he himself has learned a great deal from that tour. Even though his reference to recognition of China has been modified at various times, I believe that at some time in the not distant future Canada must recognize the government that is in fact the government of China today. With that recognition by Canada and other nations in the western world I trust will go an opening of trade and a reduction of trade barriers, because I believe that trade in peacetime goods with China, as with Russia, is in the best interests of the peoples of the world and of peace. As we all know, a conference is to take place at Geneva in April for the purpose of discussing Far Eastern matters. As a result of that discussion I hope China may be recognized and that peacetime trade with China may be resumed once again.
I believe there are other sections of this bill that could and should be of real importance to the people of Canada but those sections today are not being used. I take it that it is under that very section that there is now a restriction on the sale or export of Canadian oats to the United States.

Of course I do not know all of the decisions that might have been taken. I can only refer to the Canadian Press report that appeared in today's Montreal Gazette. I suggest to the government that unless some concrete agreement was made as to sharing of markets the result of this conference is likely to be as barren as other conferences on the same subject. I remember that on May 6 of last year, for instance, a resolution was passed unanimously by the house before the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made his trip to Washington. That resolution read as follows:
In view of the impending departure of the Prime Minister for Washington this house desires to record its opinion that further and more vigorous efforts should be made by the government to bring about the removal of the restrictions imposed by the United States on the importation of Canadian agricultural products, in violation of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
That resolution was passed unanimously by the Canadian House of Commons. The Prime Minister of Canada and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), armed with this resolution passed unanimously by parliament, went to the United States, met officials of the United States government, yes, met President Eisenhower, and asked that the United States lift the restrictions then in effect on Canadian agricultural products. As far as I know, that conference resulted in the lifting of no restrictions.
But since that time there has been further restriction, this time imposed by Canada, it is true, on the exportation of oats to the United States market.
