Export and Import Permits Act but as far as I can see all goods which might be sent to a potential enemy country must be considered strategic goods. I am not saying that we should break off any particular type of trade with our potential enemies. I believe we have got to be humanitarian in our outlook toward these things. Canada is a country which produces vast supplies of agricultural products which in the main are food products, and I believe we should attempt to dispose of our food products, if we can, to people who need them. If the people behind the iron curtain need food the humanitarian thing to do is to let them have it. But as far as I am personally concerned anything apart from food, and perhaps clothing, is a strategic material.
There is another point I would like to make while I am on my feet, and it is simply this. Once again I see no reason for dillydallying around. If we want to feed the people behind the iron curtain who may be hungry, then I believe we should do so even though, if we believe the propaganda, the iron curtain countries are the only ones with a high standard of living. We know, of course, that is not true. But if we do ship foodstuffs to iron curtain countries, as the hon. member for Assiniboia has suggested, then I believe it would be one of the best deterrents to possible war. However, that will not work if the people behind the iron curtain do not know that that food comes from Canada. What assurance have we that they would know? Is this food going to be labelled "Made in Canada"? I rather doubt it. I do not believe communist strategy would permit their people to learn that they are living on foodstuff which comes from what they would call a capitalist country.
All these things are part of the picture and I would like the parliamentary assistant to reply if he can. Perhaps my remarks have been somewhat general but I will repeat my first question: Are any other countries, apart from iron curtain countries, likely to come within this control area? The parliamentary assistant may not know, as a country which may be regarded as suitable for this list one day may not be suitable the next.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
In answer to the hon. member's tost question with respect to countries within the area control list I would say that under the bill now before us, if and when it becomes law, it is not anticipated that there will be any countries on the area control list outside the iron curtain. The situation at the present time is that the area control list, under the present legislation which is now in effect, does include a number of countries bordering on the countries behind the iron curtain and which now have to be included. But with 
the powers that are provided for in this bill we anticipate that we shall be able to eliminate all those countries from the area control list and limit it simply to the iron curtain countries.
On the second question with respect to the nature of strategic goods, of course that is a difficult question and one that is continually under review by the committee to which I have already referred. However, I can tell the hon. gentleman that no food or foodstuff that is produced in Canada and is in surplus supply in this country is on the strategic list as a commodity that cannot be exported to any part of the world.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Clause (d) of section 2 defines "minister" as meaning the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and including any person authorized by him to perform his functions. The powers of the minister under the act are very wide. For example, permits can not only be issued but can be cancelled, amended, suspended or reinstated. There are also other very wide powers. In actual practice what persons are authorized by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to exercise these functions?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: That is a power that is in the present act. The official who is authorized is the chief of the export permits branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Only the one official in the department is authorized to act as the minister or for the minister?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: That is correct.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 3-Export list of goods.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: In subclause (b) of clause 3 we find the words "to implement an intergovernmental arrangement or commitment". Will the parliamentary assistant tell the committee what governmental arrangements and/or commitments are now in existence?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: The only one, as I am informed at the moment, is the United Nations resolution relating to the shipment of arms and materials of war to Red China.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Do we not have under this category the understandings entered into between certain of the western nations apart from the United Nations resolution? I understood that the western nations had certain understandings with reference, for instance, to the definition of strategic materials. Have no agreements or arrangements been arrived at, for instance, among the NATO countries?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
I am advised no. The situation referred to by the hon. member comes under

section (a) which is regarded as related to the security of Canada and there is no firm intergovernmental arrangement or commitment that deals definitively with that particular situation. The only arrangements that can be properly described under the wording in section (b) is the United Nations resolution to which I have referred.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Then will the hon. gentleman tell us more about the existing arrangement that is based upon subclause (a) which he has just mentioned?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: The NATO countries and some other friendly nations which are not members of NATO have a committee that meets in Paris where there are discussions of the list of strategic goods; where the interests of all these countries, including Canada, are represented; and where decisions are taken in common with respect to that list. Those decisions are observed by the member governments represented on that committee.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: I presume that is a committee meeting from time to time in Paris?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: I think it is in almost continual session. It is a continuing committee.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: In Paris?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: In Paris.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will recall that in the passages I quoted last night from reports that came from London, there was one that I quoted from, as reported at page 3097 of Hansard, in which appeared these words:
... it was stated authoritatively that Britain will submit new proposals for a revision of the embargo list to the United States and France through British embassies in the two capitals.
I presume that those proposals will be submitted to all the nations which are parties to the present arrangement. Last night I asked whether the Canadian government had been consulted in this respect. Can the hon. gentleman answer that question now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Yes. That is correct. These proposals would be discussed in that committee. I am not advised as to whether or not any definite action has been taken by the British government as indicated in the quotation put on Hansard by the hon. member; but I can assure him that if those proposals have been made or if they are made in the future, they will be referred to the committee to which I have made reference.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
Can the hon. gentleman tell us what is the position of the Canadian government with reference to proposals for a revision of the embargo list?
Export and Import Permits Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: We have not seen any proposals, so far as I am aware, arising out of the statement put on Hansard by the hon. member.	.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: That is the statement under date of February 25.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: But in answer to the hon. member for Assiniboia I made it clear that our objectives were similar to those in Great Britain and that our representatives would be authorized to discuss their proposals in the light of those objectives.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: What is the situation with regard to scrap metal? I realize that it would not be permissible to export that material to countries behind the iron curtain but at one time at least there were restrictions on the export of scrap metal to the United States and possibly to other countries which are not countries behind the iron curtain. What is the position today?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: I am advised that the export of scrap is under permit. Permits are freely issued for export from eastern Canada. There are some restrictions in western Canada because of local conditions and local demands which have to be provided for.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: That hardly seems fair to western Canada. They cannot export their scrap to the United States. They cannot send it back east without paying an extremely high freight rate. Yet the scrap metal from eastern Canada can be exported to the United States. How is that discrimination justified?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: I am informed that the western dealers have no complaint. They are currently getting $23 a ton for scrap whereas the eastern price is $21 a ton. I understand that they are quite satisfied with the position at the moment.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: I am not so sure of that. I think perhaps it is a case of being satisfied because they cannot be anything else, for the government has them by the neck. But what about the export of scrap metal to Japan? Is that permitted?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Yes, I am advised that exports are permitted to Japan and that a substantial quantity has moved from Canada to Japan.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
Section 3 (c) reads as follows:
To ensure that there is an adequate supply and distribution of such article in Canada for defence or other needs.
I presume these permits are required for scrap metal on the basis of "other needs".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
Yes, I am advised that is correct.

Export and Import Permits Act

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Would there be the same power to control the export of iron ore to Japan?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Yes. I am advised there would be if it were in short supply, but I understand there is no supply problem in that connection.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
I am very glad that the parliamentary assistant has made that statement because the Minister of Trade and Commerce has told me on other occasions that he has no power whatever to control the exportation of iron ore from British Columbia to Japan. The parliamentary assistant has now admitted that there is that power under this legislation. I would point out that iron ore is not in plentiful supply in British Columbia. We have very limited reserves and we are extremely anxious to have a smelter established on the west coast and are very much afraid that if the export of iron ore to Japan in large quantities is permitted the result may be that it will never be possible to establish a steel industry on the west coast.
I have here a return made on March 9 giving the amount of iron ore exported from the west coast to Japan in 1953. The amount was 958,046 tons, nearly a million tons which, for our deposits, is a very large amount. The year before the amount was 794,311 tons. I suggest that the government look into the possibility of expanding the permit system to cover the export of iron ore so that if it is a fact that there is a shortage of iron ore on the west coast exports to Japan can then be controlled. We are in the position now that our iron ore is being exported to Japan largely in Japanese bottoms and we are buying finished steel from Japan at a price perhaps ten times or more the amount we get for the iron ore. As I understand it, at the moment the government has no permit system so far as iron ore is concerned. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: It is not under export control now.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Then I would ask that the matter be looked into and that some sort of export control be set up so that the department can at least prevent the export of iron ore to an extent that will be detrimental to the development of a steel industry on the west coast.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant a question with respect to subsection (a) which reads:
To ensure that arms, ammunition . . . will not be made available to any destination wherein their use might be detrimental to the security of Canada.
Are we to assume that once any such material leaves Canada for the designated country we have no further control over it? What I have in mind is this. Suppose, for instance, that we shipped some material to

Czechoslovakia. Have we any control at all over what that country will do with it? Is there anything to prevent Czechoslovakia from sending it to some other iron curtain country, to Hungary, let us say, or some other country-even to Russia, if you like? Are we to assume that once it gets to the country of destination we have no more control at all with respect to it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. Czechoslovakia is behind the iron curtain and we would not send arms, ammunition or anything of that kind there. There is export control on movements to that country.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: That is not a perfect illustration. Let us say we send it to some other country that is not behind the iron curtain and they do not have any such restrictive measure. It may be a good bargaining point for them to get some of our material and then trade it to some iron curtain country at a price for something they need. Is there anything to prevent that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Yes. The problem to which the hon. member refers is that of transshipment, for instance, an export from Canada to country A, which is outside the iron curtain, being received in that country and then transshipped to some country behind the iron curtain. That is a matter that is under careful and continuous study by the committee in Paris to which I referred, and one of the main purposes of the bill is to enable us to deal with acts which take place in Canada which contribute to such transshipment. That is one of the important new aspects of our control mechanism that we are establishing by this bill.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: In other words, the effective control is to determine the reliability of the shipper to start with. If he is not reliable you will not licence him. If he proves unreliable after he has a licence then you have recourse to the penalty provided in the act and you can take away his licence for the future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Yes. In general terms that is correct.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Has the parliamentary assistant got figures as to the scrap metal exported to Japan in 1953?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: No. I am informed we have not got those figures. We can get them for the hon. member. I am also informed that the exports of scrap to Japan have been what is known as distant scrap, scrap that cannot be moved to Vancouver economically to be sold in the market there.

Clause agreed to.

On clause 4-Export list of countries.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Clause 4 relates to the establishment of a list of countries to be called an area control list. I referred last night to the list of countries established under order in council of January 13, 1953, as set out in the first column on page 3096 of Hansard. Has there been any change in the list of countries since that date? In the second place, is any further change now in contemplation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: I am advised that there has not been any change in the list since that date, but there are very extensive changes contemplated if and when the present bill comes into force. As I explained to the hon. member for Macleod, when the bill comes into force we foresee the possibility of eliminating all countries from that list except those that are actually behind the iron curtain.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Does that mean that Hong Kong will be dropped from the list? It has a peculiar and special position as the commercial gateway to China.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: That is a special case. We do not know whether or not it can be eliminated but that matter will receive consideration.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 5-Import list of goods.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: On clause 5, I wonder whether the parliamentary assistant might inform the committee what goods are on the import control list because of the scarceness of the article in world markets? In other words, what commodities are on the import control list under (a) and then what commodities, if any, are on the import control list under (b), which is to implement any action taken under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. the Fisheries Prices Support Act, the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act or the Agricultural Products Board Act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: In answer to the hon. member's first question there are no items on the list because of scarcity, and there is one item on the list under (b) and that is butter.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: What act does that come under? Is it carrying out the Agricultural Prices Support Act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: It is the Agricultural Prices Support Act, I understand.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
Can the parliamentary assistant tell us whether this import control list is to be a list of goods for which import licences are to be granted or a list for which import licences are to be refused?
Eocport and Import Permits Act If it is for those to be granted, would he tell us how it will achieve the purpose of the act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: In actual fact, Mr. Chairman, the list includes items in both categories.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Can the parliamentary assistant tell us how an item which appears on the list as one for which import licences are going to be granted under subsection (b) will ensure the best possible supply and distribution of that article? How is the granting of a licence going to improve the situation beyond the position which would be obtained if a person were free to import it without a licence?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
I am informed in some
instances it is necessary to establish a quota, that is a ceiling, on imports. For that reason an article would be included in the list.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: I would point out that the purpose of paragraph (a) is to ensure the best possible supply. Presumably that would be the most plentiful supply.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I
could explain by giving the hon. member an example. When sulphur was in short supply in the world it was placed on the list of imports and permits were granted in order to see that sulphur got to the essential users, for instance, defence industries and that sort of thing.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
So it was not to
control the import; it was to control the distribution after it came into the country?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: No, it was to control imports as well because there was an international arrangement with respect to the distribution of the world supply of sulphur.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
I want to say a word about clause 5 dealing with imports. I think the case for exports, prima facie, seems reasonable. We all recognize the necessity of restricting the export of strategic materials. I find myself, therefore, somewhat sympathetic to the export part of this bill. However, to use a slang phrase, I am absolutely from Missouri with regard to the import part of it.
The clause, of course, begins with these words to which we have grown so accustomed that even we in the opposition do not resist them as much as we should. It reads:
The governor in council may establish a list of goods, to be called an import control list, including therein any article the import of which he deems it necessary to control for any of the following purposes . . .
I want to recall to our minds what these very simple words mean, because we are apt to forget. What that means is that four

Export and Import Permits Act men, because I understand that four is a quorum of the cabinet, can establish a list of goods and put on a restriction against the import of them. It means if you are in the importing business your business can be ruined by a decision of which you know nothing, and of which there is no publicity until it suddenly comes down on you. Then, you find you are the victim of it. There is no appeal from it.
We all know there have to be orders in council, but I do not think we should allow ourselves to take them as the ordinary course of business. I think we should always expect to be satisfied how far they are necessary. Let us look at this clause on that basis. I noticed that in his remarks on March 16, page 3067 of Hansard, the parliamentary assistant seemed to take for granted that he needed

to say nothing about paragraphs (a) and (b) of this clause. He confined himself almost entirely to paragraph (c), which is new. I read what he said:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
It is ten o'clock; how about reading it tomorrow.
Clause stands.
Progress reported.
